clue.text: Red Shadow's solo in the musical

definitions.text: Red Shadow's solo in the musical

parts.words: Red Shadow's solo in the musical
parts.note: the Red Shadow is the masked hero of the operetta The Desert Song, and his famous solo number is a song whose title also describes a soloist

explanation.surface: A question about which song a character sings on his own in a stage show.
explanation.walkthrough: The Desert Song (Romberg, 1926) has its hero, the Red Shadow, sing this ballad; the title also says what any solo is: a single performer by himself.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the title of the hero's best-known ballad in The Desert Song, and a solo is literally one performer by himself.

clue.text: To upset Enid with so little money is immoral

indicators.note: to upset something is to knock it about, so the letters of the name are jumbled

parts.note: a cent is a coin of trifling value, a tiny sum of money

explanation.surface: Someone thinks it wrong to leave poor Enid so short of cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To upset' turns ENID into INDE; CENT follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Something indecent offends against accepted standards of behaviour, so it is improper or immoral.

clue.text: Weep and get fat

explanation.surface: Advice to cry and put on weight.
explanation.definitionFit: To sob noisily is to bawl like a child; the noun is the thick insulating layer under a whale's skin.

clue.text: Bind a blow he sustains

parts.note: a swat is a sharp slapping blow
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man receives a blow and has to be bandaged up.
explanation.definitionFit: To swathe is to wrap or bandage something round, binding it in cloth.

clue.text: Edward partly submerged in my river

indicators.note: something submerged goes under and is enclosed, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: only part of the name is used, its opening letters

explanation.surface: Edward is half under water in the speaker's own river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'partly' takes EDWA from Edward, and 'submerged in' puts it inside MY. The Medway is a river in Kent, south-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: The Medway is a river flowing through Kent into the Thames estuary.

clue.text: Malaysian advocates? No, but the name sticks

definitions.text: Malaysian advocates? No, but the name sticks

parts.words: Malaysian advocates? No, but the name sticks
parts.note: the name looks like barristers from a Malaysian island, but it is the name given to a kind of walking stick, a heavy cane

explanation.surface: Asks whether certain lawyers from Malaysia are meant, then says the name belongs to something else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sticks' is a noun: this is the name of a knobbed walking cane made from a palm, once said to be used to settle disputes on the island of Penang.
explanation.definitionFit: These are heavy palm-wood walking canes, so named jokily as the way Penang residents settled lawsuits.

clue.text: Let-down for railwaymen on the pools?

definitions.text: Let-down for railwaymen on the pools?

parts.words: Let-down for railwaymen on the pools?
parts.note: a breakdown of the movable track switches lets railway staff down, and a coupon that scores too little on football pools is a let-down too

explanation.surface: Railway workers who bet on football coupons are disappointed.
explanation.walkthrough: On the railways points are the track switches; on the football pools (a British weekly betting coupon) points are what a forecast scores.
explanation.definitionFit: On a railway a breakdown of track switches causes delays; on the pools, scoring too low means no win.

clue.text: One's personal disregard of low accommodation with fleas all over the place

indicators.note: things all over the place are scattered in disorder, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: a basement is a flat or room below ground level, the lowest lodging in a house

explanation.surface: A flea-ridden cellar flat that someone lives in with no self-respect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all over the place' turns FLEAS into SELFA, which goes before BASEMENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Self-abasement is humbling or belittling oneself, a disregard for one's own dignity.

clue.text: Change gear on the motorway, reflectively it appears

indicators.note: in this across clue one piece is placed on, meaning after, the other

parts.note: the M1 is the main motorway north from London, written MI in crosswords

indicators.note: to change the gear is to rework it, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Driving instructions about shifting gear on a motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change' rearranges GEAR into RAGE, placed 'on' (after) MI, the M1, Britain's first long motorway.
explanation.definitionFit: A mirage is an optical illusion caused by light bending, so something appears as if reflected that is not there.

clue.text: Laconic message from Mary Stuart's eloping partner?

explanation.surface: A brief note sent by the Scottish queen's lover.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as two words it is a terse report that the pair are fine; whole, it is the Earl who carried off Mary Queen of Scots and married her.
explanation.definitionFit: A two-word note says the pair are fine; James Hepburn, the Earl, abducted Mary Queen of Scots and married her in 1567.

clue.text: Pen mate

parts.note: a pen is a female swan, so her mate is the male swan, not a friend by letter

explanation.surface: Looks like a pen pal, someone you write to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pen' is the female swan, not a writing tool.
explanation.definitionFit: Male swans pair with females called pens, so the male bird is the pen's partner.

clue.text: Smooth oarsman

explanation.surface: Praise for a rower's polished style.
explanation.definitionFit: To stroke is to run a hand gently over something to smooth it; the rower nearest the stern who sets the rhythm is also named so.

clue.text: May never be arranged for anybody

indicators.note: letters that are arranged are set out in a new order

explanation.surface: Something that can never be organised to suit everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'be arranged' rearranges MAYNEVER; 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The everyman is the ordinary typical person, standing for anyone at all.

clue.text: Ridicule a cut from the butcher

explanation.surface: Making fun of a joint of meat.
explanation.definitionFit: To rib is to tease or mock; a rib is also a joint of beef sold by butchers.

clue.text: Produces one's own goods

explanation.surface: Someone manufacturing their own merchandise.
explanation.definitionFit: To effect is to bring about or cause; personal effects are belongings.

clue.text: About half your dog!

parts.note: C is short for circa, Latin for about, used before approximate dates

indicators.note: only half of the word is used, here its second two letters

explanation.surface: A remark that someone's dog is roughly halved.
explanation.walkthrough: C (circa) then 'half' of YOUR, its back half UR.
explanation.definitionFit: A cur is a mongrel or worthless dog.

clue.text: Free translation of braille

indicators.note: a translation renders words into another form, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Turning Braille into print without strict accuracy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'translation of' rearranges BRAILLE; the surface suggests a loose rendering.
explanation.definitionFit: Liberal means generous or unrestricted, as in a free or loose translation.

clue.text: In a fix at the Pole

definitions.text: In a fix at the Pole

parts.words: In a fix at the Pole
parts.note: a ship stuck fast in polar sea ice is literally fixed in place, rather than in difficulties

explanation.surface: An explorer in trouble at the North or South Pole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fix' means held fast, as a ship frozen in pack ice, not a predicament.
explanation.definitionFit: A vessel trapped by frozen sea in polar waters cannot move, so it is held fast.

clue.text: Natural gift? Yes, in a certain number

indicators.note: one piece is placed in, inside, the other

parts.note: eight is a particular number
taken as written

explanation.surface: Agreeing that some talent belongs to a given number of people.
explanation.walkthrough: YES goes 'in' EIGHT, after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The ability to see is a faculty one is born with, a natural endowment.

clue.text: Doesn't go out with nautical guys

parts.note: stays are the ropes or wires bracing a ship's mast, guy ropes on board
in can mean with or among, as in someone in the crowd

explanation.surface: Someone avoids a night out with sailors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'guys' are ropes, not men: on a ship stays are ropes supporting a mast.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who remains at home does not go out for the evening.

clue.text: Tactful about secret i'd recalled before

indicators.note: one piece comes before the other in the answer
recalled means called back, so this short word is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written, without the apostrophe

indicators.note: letters knocked about are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone tactful about a secret they earlier confided.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recalled' reverses ID into DI; 'about' turns SECRET into SCREET; DI comes 'before'.
explanation.definitionFit: A discreet person is careful in speech and keeps confidences, showing tact.

clue.text: Embraces about fifty snakes

parts.note: C is short for circa, Latin for about
L is the Roman numeral for fifty
asps are small venomous snakes

explanation.surface: Someone hugs around fifty snakes.
explanation.definitionFit: To clasp someone is to hold them tightly in one's arms, a hug.

clue.text: Outstanding man no side takes up

indicators.note: in a down clue taking up means raising from the bottom, so the words are read upward, backwards

explanation.surface: A remarkable man joins neither faction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes up' reverses NOSIDE in this down clue. Thomas Edison was the American inventor.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Edison, inventor of the phonograph and light bulb, was a man of exceptional achievement.

clue.text: The Spanish uniform side

parts.note: el is the Spanish masculine form of the
even means regular or consistent, the same throughout

explanation.surface: The Spanish team wears matching kit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'side' is a team: football and cricket teams have this many players.
explanation.definitionFit: A football or cricket team fields this many players, so the team is named by its number.

clue.text: Good investment for a pound

parts.note: lb is the abbreviation of libra, the pound weight

explanation.surface: Advice about investing well for a pound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good investment' means holy vesture, an in-vestment: the alb is a priest's white vestment.
explanation.definitionFit: An alb is a white ankle-length robe worn by clergy at Mass, so a holy garment.

clue.text: Kindness shown by Aunty smothering him

indicators.note: smothering suggests one thing smothered and mixed up with another, so the letters are rearranged together

explanation.surface: Aunty's kindness is shown by smothering a boy with hugs.
explanation.walkthrough: AUNTY and HIM are rearranged together, with 'smothering' as the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Humanity is compassion and benevolence toward others.

clue.text: Roland's smatch-and who could ask for more!

explanation.surface: Mentions a legendary knight's equal, then a boy who wanted more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A Roland for an Oliver' (two Charlemagne paladins) means a match; Dickens's Oliver Twist asked for more gruel.
explanation.definitionFit: Roland and his fellow paladin were equals in combat; Dickens's workhouse orphan famously asked for more food.

clue.text: A blast from the bunker

parts.note: suggests an explosion from a military shelter, but means a golf stroke that blasts the ball out of a sand trap

explanation.surface: Gunfire or a bomb going off from a fortified shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bunker' is a golf sand trap, not a wartime shelter.
explanation.definitionFit: Golfers hit through the sand behind the ball, sending sand and ball out together in a burst.
